pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Measuring Earthquake Strength — scientists use a seismometer to detect and record ground shaking; earthquakes release energy that travels outward as waves; and a magnitude scale gives a number for an earthquake's strength.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement):** In England this is KS2 **Geography** enrichment (earthquakes), not KS2 science. Wave/energy formalism and measurement are DfE **KS3** (physics waves; Geography hazards). Frame as 'how do we measure something we can't see?'.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No dedicated elementary PE; earthquakes as measured hazards connect to **4-ESS3-2** (monitoring/reducing impacts) and the wave/energy detail to **MS-PS4** and **MS-ESS**. Reading a magnitude number is a data-interpretation (SEP) skill. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisites 'Why Earthquakes Happen' and 'Ring of Fire'. Three linked ideas: a seismometer works because a heavy mass stays still (inertia) while the ground and frame move under it, tracing a record; the earthquake's energy spreads OUT as waves that shake the seismometer; and magnitude summarises strength as a single number — with the crucial subtlety that each step up the scale is a BIG jump (roughly ten times the shaking amplitude, far more energy), so a magnitude 6 is not just '20% more' than a 5. Keep the log idea intuitive, not computational.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (early-formal; instrument model + a non-linear scale). Children grasp 'a machine records shaking' but often read magnitude as a linear ruler and confuse the CAUSE's strength with the shaking FELT at a place. Success = explain what a seismometer records, describe energy travelling as waves, and read a magnitude number as strength (bigger number = much stronger).
bestPractices: Make the seismometer's principle concrete via inertia: a suspended heavy mass with a pen stays still while the ground/paper moves under it, drawing the wiggly trace — model it physically (a weight on a spring over a moving strip).
Show the record (seismogram) as the DATA: bigger wiggles = stronger shaking; teach children to read amplitude qualitatively.
Confront the linear-scale misconception gently: each whole number up the magnitude scale means roughly ten times the shaking and much more energy — use a visual step-jump, not arithmetic.
Separate magnitude (the earthquake's size at the source, one number) from intensity (how strongly it's felt at a given place, which varies with distance) — a common conflation.
Link to prior topics: the waves are the energy released when rocks snapped (Why Earthquakes Happen), spreading out from the source and fading with distance.
keyRepresentations: Suspended-mass seismometer model (inertia: mass stays still, ground moves, pen traces)
Seismogram trace — amplitude of wiggles as a read-out of shaking strength
A magnitude 'staircase' where each step is a ~10× jump in shaking (non-linear)
Ripples spreading and shrinking from the source — waves fading with distance
commonMisconceptions: The magnitude scale is linear (a 6 is only a bit more than a 5) — in fact each step is ~10× the shaking amplitude and far more energy.
A seismometer 'feels' the quake like a person (it works by a heavy mass staying still by inertia while the frame/ground moves).
Magnitude and how strongly you FEEL it are the same (magnitude is the source size; felt intensity depends on distance and ground).
Earthquake energy travels in straight lines to one place (it spreads outward as waves in all directions, fading with distance).
Bigger wiggles on the trace always mean a bigger earthquake regardless of distance (distance matters; scientists account for it).

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, build understanding of how scientists measure earthquakes: a seismometer records ground shaking using a heavy mass that stays nearly still by inertia while the frame and paper move under it; earthquake energy spreads outward as waves that fade with distance; and a magnitude scale gives one number for an earthquake's strength, where each whole step up is a BIG jump: the recorded waves are roughly ten times bigger when compared at the same distance (not a linear notch), and much more energy is released. Keep the log idea intuitive, never computational. Core activity: a shakeable seismometer model with a live trace, a magnitude dial that visibly multiplies the wiggles, and a distance control that separates magnitude (the quake's true size) from how strongly a place feels it. Reference diagrams, quiz-based consolidation, and an optional 3D view are preserved as distinct supports.

activities.title: Shake a seismometer and read the trace
feedback: If a learner thinks the machine senses or feels the shaking: point out the mass barely moves — it is the frame and paper that move under it, and that difference is what draws the line.
If they read any wiggle as 'an earthquake' regardless of size: compare a gentle and a hard shake and have them rank the traces by wiggle size.
Reinforce: bigger wiggles (bigger amplitude) = stronger shaking at that spot.
activities.rationale: Enacting the inertia principle and watching the live trace respond makes concrete why a still mass records motion, directly confronting the 'the machine feels it' misconception. A physical weight-on-a-spring over a moving strip is a welcome concrete realisation; a screen model offers a live amplitude read-out.
sourceClaims: A seismometer records ground motion using a suspended mass that remains nearly still by inertia while the frame moves with the ground; earthquake energy travels outward as seismic waves.
learnerActions: Shake a model ground (physically with a weight hanging on a spring over a moving paper strip, or with an on-screen shake control) with quick, sharp shakes and watch the suspended heavy mass lag behind and stay nearly still while the frame and paper move under it (in a homemade model it may still swing or bob a little, and slow shakes can carry it along).
Watch the attached pen draw a live wiggly trace (a seismogram) and say in your own words why a mass that stays still can record motion: the GROUND and paper move, not the mass — that is inertia.
Shake harder and gentler and describe how the size (amplitude) of the wiggles changes: bigger wiggles mean stronger shaking.
Point to the parts and label them: the heavy mass (stays nearly still), the frame (moves with the ground), the pen, and the paper record.
activities.intendedInsight: A seismometer does not 'feel' a quake like a person; it works because a heavy suspended mass stays nearly still by inertia while everything else moves under it, tracing a record whose wiggle size shows how strong the shaking is.

activities.title: The magnitude staircase: each step is a big jump
feedback: If a learner expects a small change from 5 to 6: replay the step and have them compare the before/after wiggle heights side by side.
If they try to do arithmetic (e.g. '20% more'): steer back to the visual — count how many times taller the new wiggles are, not the difference in numbers.
Confirm: one step up on the scale is a BIG jump, with waves roughly ten times bigger on the trace at the same distance.
activities.rationale: Manipulating the dial and seeing the trace and energy meter leap gives a visceral, non-computational sense of the logarithmic scale, gently confronting the linear-ruler misconception. The energy meter and amplitude leap are optional illustrative mechanisms that make the jump vivid.
sourceClaims: The moment magnitude scale is logarithmic: each whole-number step corresponds to ~10× greater shaking amplitude and roughly 32× more energy release.
learnerActions: Before changing anything, predict: 'How much bigger is the shaking from a magnitude 6 than a magnitude 5 — a little, or a lot?'

Keeping the seismometer at the same distance, turn a magnitude dial from 5 up to 6 (or use a visual step-staircase) and watch the trace amplitude leap roughly ten times bigger, with a released-energy meter jumping far more.
Step up again (6 to 7) and describe the pattern in words: each whole number means waves about ten times bigger on the trace (at the same distance), not 'one more'.
State the correction to a friend who says 'a 7 is just one more than a 6': no — measured at the same distance, a 7 makes waves about ten times bigger than a 6, and releases far more energy.
activities.intendedInsight: The magnitude scale is not like ordinary counting: each whole-number step means roughly ten times greater recorded wave amplitude when compared at the same distance (and much more energy released), so a magnitude 7 is vastly stronger than a 6.

activities.title: Same quake, different places: magnitude vs felt intensity
feedback: If a learner says magnitude is bigger near the epicentre and smaller far away: separate the two ideas — the magnitude number stays the same; it is the shaking you FEEL that fades with distance.
If they assume a bigger magnitude always means more damage: note that damage also depends on distance, depth, ground type and how buildings are built — not magnitude alone.
Reinforce: one earthquake = one magnitude everywhere; the felt intensity varies from place to place.
activities.rationale: Varying distance while magnitude stays fixed makes the magnitude-vs-intensity distinction tangible and links to the prior 'Why Earthquakes Happen' idea of energy released by snapping rocks. Reading smaller wiggles farther away also guards against 'bigger wiggles always mean a bigger quake'.
sourceClaims: A seismometer records ground motion using a suspended mass that remains nearly still by inertia while the frame moves with the ground; earthquake energy travels outward as seismic waves.
learnerActions: With one fixed earthquake set, drag a distance control (or move a marker) to place a seismometer nearer and farther from the source, and watch the trace get smaller with distance.
Explain why people nearby feel the quake strongly while people far away barely notice it: the waves spread outward and fade with distance.
Answer: does moving farther away change the earthquake's MAGNITUDE, or only how strongly you FEEL it? (It changes only the felt intensity; magnitude is one fixed number for the quake.)
Connect to what you already know: the waves are the energy released when rocks snapped, spreading out in all directions from the source and shrinking as they go.
activities.intendedInsight: Magnitude is a single fixed number describing the earthquake's size at its source (from the energy released), while felt intensity depends on distance (and ground and buildings) and fades the farther away you are.

activities.title: Reference: label the seismometer and the seismogram
feedback: If a part is mislabelled: re-reveal its role (e.g. the mass stays still; the frame moves).
If a learner reads magnitude off a trace as if it were linear: direct them to the ~10× reveal.
activities.rationale: A labelled diagram and annotated seismogram are strong reference material that explain the parts clearly, but a static reference cannot enact the live trace or the step-jump; use it alongside the manipulable model, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: A seismometer records ground motion using a suspended mass that remains nearly still by inertia while the frame moves with the ground; earthquake energy travels outward as seismic waves.
learnerActions: Study a labelled seismometer cutaway and tap or point to each part: the suspended mass (reveal 'stays still — inertia'), the frame, the pen, the paper.
Examine an annotated seismogram and mark where the wiggles are biggest (largest amplitude = strongest shaking).
Open a 'Is a 6 just a bit more than a 5?' flap or note and read the ~10× reveal in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming the parts of a seismometer and reading amplitude on a seismogram gives a clear reference model that supports, but does not replace, the hands-on trace-building.

activities.title: Check and consolidate
feedback: Full response: explains each step means about ten times bigger waves (compared at the same distance) AND that magnitude is one fixed number while felt intensity fades with distance.
Partial: gets one idea (e.g. the 7 is much bigger) but still confuses magnitude with felt intensity, or vice versa — reteach the missing half.
Gap: treats magnitude as linear and thinks it changes with location — return to the staircase and distance activities.
activities.rationale: The two-part diagnostic is discriminating because it targets two independent traps at once (linear scale, and magnitude-vs-intensity); a learner holding either misconception gets one part wrong. These tasks consolidate and assess rather than first reveal the concepts.
sourceClaims: The moment magnitude scale is logarithmic: each whole-number step corresponds to ~10× greater shaking amplitude and roughly 32× more energy release.
learnerActions: Order a set of seismograms from smallest to largest amplitude (weakest to strongest shaking).
Answer: 'How much bigger is the shaking from a magnitude 6 than a magnitude 5?' and justify with the step-jump idea.

Respond to the two-part prompt: 'A friend says a magnitude 7 is just a little bit (about one) stronger than a 6 — is that right? And does the same earthquake have the same magnitude whether you are on top of it or far away? Explain.'
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who has grasped the ideas can read traces by amplitude, state that each step is about ten times stronger, and separate the fixed magnitude from the distance-dependent felt intensity.

constraints: Keep the logarithmic idea intuitive and visual (step-jumps, leaping wiggles), not arithmetic — these learners should feel 'much bigger', not compute 10× or 32×.
Prerequisites: 'Why Earthquakes Happen' and 'Ring of Fire'. The waves are the energy released when rocks snapped.

Standards placement is mixed: in England this is KS2 Geography enrichment, with wave/energy formalism and measurement being KS3; in the US it connects to NGSS 4-ESS3-2 (monitoring/reducing hazards) with wave/energy detail at middle school (MS-PS4 / MS-ESS). Reading a magnitude number is a data-interpretation skill. Do not teach the formal wave/energy equations at this age.

A labelled diagram or seismogram is a reference scaffold: it explains parts and lets learners read amplitude, but it cannot enact the live trace or the step-jump; pair it with a manipulable or physical model for the dynamic insight.
Recognition/ordering and multiple-choice tasks consolidate and assess but do not by themselves elicit independent explanation; also ask learners to explain in their own words.
The energy meter, magnitude dial, distance slider and tap-to-reveal flaps are optional illustrative mechanisms to make the mechanism concrete — not mandatory, and not product-specific requirements.
Optional extension: a 3D seismometer the child can shake and view from any angle may show the mass-and-frame motion in space, but the principle reads clearly in 2D — this is polish, not required.
Avoid implying bigger wiggles always mean a bigger earthquake regardless of distance: distance (and depth, ground, building quality) matter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row (USGS seismometer/inertia claim and the USGS logarithmic-scale claim); the ~10×-amplitude and ~32×-energy figures are presented as claims carried from the source, not independently re-checked here.

The source states the moment magnitude scale is logarithmic with ~32× more energy per step; the learner-facing material deliberately keeps only the intuitive '~10× shaking, much more energy' framing to avoid computation at this age — the 32× figure is retained in a consolidation sourceClaim but not taught as arithmetic.

The original row's artefact-fit notes asserted that a static image 'can't enact' the insight and a quiz 'tests rather than reveals'; these have been softened to scope-limited affordance statements rather than universal claims that only one medium can teach.
The physical weight-on-a-spring model and card/paper strip are approximations of an idealised seismometer; treat them as models of the real instrument.

probeDeeper: About how much bigger is the shaking in a magnitude 7 than a magnitude 6 — a bit, or a lot?
If one earthquake happens, why might people nearby feel it strongly but people far away barely notice?
Does moving further from an earthquake change its magnitude, or just how much you feel it?
What does a seismometer actually record, and how does that give a magnitude?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the scale isn't like ordinary counting. Each step up is about TEN times bigger shaking (and much more energy), so a magnitude 7 is vastly stronger than a 6, not 'one more'. And magnitude is a single number for the earthquake itself (from the energy released where the rocks broke) — it doesn't change with where you stand. What changes with distance is how strongly you FEEL it (the intensity), which fades the further away you are.

errorPatterns.pattern: The magnitude scale is like normal counting — a 7 is just one more than a 6
errorPatterns.nextMove: Each step is about 10x the shaking; show the jump in wiggle size on a seismogram.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — a 7 is just a little bit (about one) stronger than a 6.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the steps as equal / linear.

errorPatterns.pattern: The same earthquake has different magnitudes depending on where you are
errorPatterns.nextMove: Magnitude is one fixed number for the quake; it's the felt INTENSITY that fades with distance.
errorPatterns.distractor: The magnitude is bigger if you're near it and smaller if you're far away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the magnitude is bigger near the epicentre and smaller far away.

errorPatterns.pattern: A bigger magnitude number always means more damage, no matter what
errorPatterns.nextMove: Damage also depends on distance, depth and how buildings are built — not magnitude alone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ignores depth, distance, ground and building quality.

responseLevels.gap: Treats magnitude as linear and thinks it changes with location.
responseLevels.full: Explains each magnitude step is about ten times bigger shaking, and that magnitude is a single fixed number for the quake (from energy released) while the felt intensity fades with distance — read from a seismometer.
responseLevels.partial: Gets one idea (e.g. that a 7 is much bigger) but still confuses magnitude with felt intensity, or vice versa.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A magnitude 7 earthquake and a magnitude 6 earthquake — a friend says 'the 7 is just a little bit stronger, about one more'. Is that right? And does the same earthquake have the same magnitude whether you're right on top of it or far away? Explain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two independent traps: treating the scale as linear, and confusing the fixed magnitude with felt intensity. Asking both forces the ~10x-per-step idea AND the magnitude-vs-intensity split; a child holding either misconception gets one part wrong.
